source.title_on_document: Who Owns Creativity and Who Does the Work? Trade-offs in LLM-Supported Research Ideation

supplement.where: Appendices A-F are included in this PDF, pp. 23-32. No separate supplementary-file URL is specified.
supplement.holds: Agent prompts and RAG implementation (Appendix A); pilot RAG and AI-system comparisons (Appendix B, pp. 27-28, Tables 6-7); moderation/task/interview protocol (Appendix C, pp. 28-29); a representative use case (Appendix D, pp. 29-30); participant demographics (Appendix E, p. 31, Table 8); additional statistics (Appendix F, pp. 30-32), including Tukey HSD differences, p-values, and interval bounds for Prompt_full_proposal and Select_improvements in Tables 9-10 and creativity-support/effort correlations in Figure 8. These additional tables do not supply pairwise uncertainty for the unique-proposal fluency outcome.

paper_design_summary: Researchers were randomly assigned to Low, Medium, or Intensive control of ResearchGuru in supervised Zoom sessions; 51 people were analyzed after exclusions using logged proposal counts and self-reported creativity support, effort, and ownership (pp. 11-14, Sections 5-6). Two development evaluations compared initial AI-generated drafts with versus without RAG and across AI systems using human and model judgments (pp. 27-28, Appendix B). A separate within-person protocol-development pilot informed the formal procedure but supplies no scored creative-output results or identifiable analyzed sample size (p. 11, Section 4.2).

studies.label: Formal user study: Low, Medium, and Intensive control of research-ideation agents

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual researchers were assigned to one of three AI control configurations. Sessions were supervised remotely through Zoom screen sharing; recruitment was through academic networks, not an online panel. The randomization procedure is not specified.
assignment.quote: During the user study, participants were randomly assigned to Low, Medium, or Intensive control levels while using the system to develop research ideas across all proposal stages.
assignment.locator: p. 11, Section 5.1; p. 12, Section 5.2 (supervised Zoom sessions)

arms.name: Low
arms.description: Researchers provide keywords and generate, select, and customize seed ideas; subsequent literature selection, proposal writing, critique, and revision are automated, without steering the Writer or Evaluator. p. 8, Table 3 and Section 3.3.1.

arms.name: Medium
arms.description: Researchers select literature, prompt section-level revisions, customize evaluation criteria, and select agent-suggested improvements; direct text editing, inline revision, and feedback on agent critiques are unavailable. p. 8, Table 3 and Section 3.3.1.

arms.name: Intensive
arms.description: Researchers have the Medium features plus direct content edits, inline text prompting, feedback on agent critiques, and customization of suggested improvements. p. 8, Table 3 and Section 3.3.1.

participants.exclusions: Three survey responses were excluded using Isolation Forest anomaly detection: two unusually low ratings and one unusually high rating. Quantitative outcomes were analyzed for 51 people, 17 per arm (p. 13, Section 5.3.1). The document reports 54 recruited people and a target allocation of 18 per arm (p. 12, Section 5.2), but does not separately report actual counts at random assignment; n_randomized is therefore null. The final number of interviews analyzed is not explicitly given.
participants.who: Active academic researchers recruited through universities and academic networks by snowball sampling; screened for recent publications and prior research use of LLMs. The recruited sample, before the quantitative exclusions, comprised 40 PhD students, 7 postdoctoral fellows, and 7 professors or research scientists (p. 12, Section 5.2).
participants.country: Recruited sample: 47 based in the United States and 7 elsewhere (p. 12, Section 5.2); Table 8 lists Jamaica, France, Korea, Canada, Germany, and India among the other locations (p. 31). Locations of the retained sample are not separately reported.
participants.quote: This resulted in 51 valid data points, with 17 for each control level.
participants.locator: p. 13, Section 5.3.1 (exclusions and analyzed counts); p. 12, Section 5.2 (recruitment and demographics); p. 31, Appendix E, Table 8

ai_tool.name_model: ResearchGuru: GPT-4.1 for Ideator and Writer; Claude Sonnet 3.7 for Evaluator
ai_tool.how_used: Integrated research-ideation and proposal-writing workflow: generate seed ideas, retrieve and synthesize literature, draft research goals and study plans, critique proposals, and revise. Human steering varies by arm. The notebook-style interface explicitly excludes a chat feature, so this is not coded open_chat. p. 8, Section 3.3.1 and Table 3; p. 10, Section 3.3.2 and Figure 2 caption.

task.description: Generate new research ideas in the researcher's own area and develop them into proposals containing literature synthesis, research goals, and a study plan. Participants save satisfactory drafts and subsequently choose their best draft. AI remains available throughout production. pp. 11-12, Section 5.1; p. 29, Appendix C.2.
task.duration: Main procedure reports approximately 90 minutes total, including 20 minutes of familiarization, 35-40 minutes of proposal generation, 5 minutes of survey, and 20-30 minutes of interview (pp. 11-12, Section 5.1). Appendix C.2 instead instructs participants to work for 30 minutes (p. 29); this discrepancy is preserved.

outcomes.name: Unique research proposals produced per hour (# Unique_research_proposals)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Log-derived participant-level count of unique research proposals, coded as output fluency because Section 6.1 explicitly describes the proposals participants created. Table 4 reports means and SDs based on function uses per hour; this stated normalization is retained. The operational rule distinguishing unique proposals from revisions is not specified. This is output quantity, not rated novelty or quality. The paper reports a three-arm one-way ANOVA and no pairwise test for this outcome (p. 12, Section 5.3.1; p. 13, Section 6.1; p. 14, Table 4).

This is not a pairwise test; no pairwise test, confidence interval, standard error, or standardized effect is printed for this outcome.

studies.label: Development evaluation: paired RAG versus non-RAG proposal drafts

assignment.what_was_assigned: The same seed ideas were expanded with and without RAG. Researchers supplied keywords and judged model-generated drafts. No allocation of people to assistance conditions or randomization of generation/presentation order is described; absence of a randomization statement does not establish that the order was nonrandom (p. 27, Appendix B.1).
assignment.quote: Each seed idea was expanded by the Writer, with and without RAG, producing two proposal drafts.

arms.name: RAG
arms.description: GPT-4o-mini Writer expands a seed idea with retrieval augmentation; paired with the non-RAG version of the same seed idea. p. 27, Appendix B.1.

arms.name: Non-RAG
arms.description: The same model expands the same seed idea without retrieval augmentation. p. 27, Appendix B.1.

participants.who: Two PhD students who supplied research keywords and evaluated generated drafts: one member of the research team with creativity expertise and one external researcher specializing in conversational agents. These are human evaluators, not two participants in a randomized assistance experiment. Each supplied keywords yielding five seed ideas; the study reports ten seed ideas in total. p. 27, Appendix B.1.
participants.quote: Two PhD students participated: one from our research team with expertise in creativity and one external researcher specializing in conversational agents (CAs).

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4o-mini generation; Claude 3.7, DeepSeek-V3, and Gemini 2.0 as judges
ai_tool.how_used: The Ideator generated seed ideas from researcher keywords, and the Writer generated paired proposal drafts with and without RAG. Humans and three LLM judges compared the drafts after in-text citations were removed. Coded other because this is a model-output evaluation, rather than provision of AI examples for a subsequently scored human creative task (p. 27, Appendix B.1).

task.description: Generate and expand field-specific research ideas into initial proposal drafts, comparing retrieval-augmented and non-retrieval versions. p. 27, Appendix B.1.

outcomes.name: Human preference between RAG and non-RAG proposal drafts
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Researchers compared the initial RAG and non-RAG drafts for the same seed idea after in-text citations were removed. They chose a better proposal or were undecided. Section 4.1 describes novelty, feasibility, and impact as joint evaluation criteria; Appendix B.1 also discusses factuality and narrative cohesion. Only a single overall preference is reported, not separate scores on those criteria. These are judgments of AI-generated drafts in a backend system test, not effects of randomly assigning people to AI assistance. Ten matched seed-idea comparisons are shown (pp. 11, 27-28). Coded usefulness under the codebook definition that includes output quality; this is a joint quality preference, not a separately measured feasibility or novelty score.

contrasts.reported: Human researchers preferred RAG in four cases, non-RAG in two, and were undecided in four. Table 6 identifies RAG preferences for ideas 2, 4, 7, and 8; non-RAG preferences for ideas 1 and 3; and undecided judgments for ideas 5, 6, 9, and 10. Direction describes the preference counts only; no inferential test or uncertainty is reported. The direction denotes more observed preferences for RAG overall, not a statistically established difference or a preference in every case.
contrasts.locator: p. 27, Appendix B.1; p. 28, Table 6; p. 11, Section 4.1 (joint evaluation criteria)

outcomes.name: LLM-judge preference between RAG and non-RAG proposal drafts
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Claude 3.7, DeepSeek-V3, and Gemini 2.0 judged the same matched RAG/non-RAG drafts, selecting the better proposal or undecided. Judge variants are kept in one outcome. These are evaluations of AI-generated outputs, not human creative performance. Ten seed-idea comparisons are reported; they are not ten participants, and multiple model judgments are not independent people (pp. 27-28, Appendix B.1 and Table 6). Coded usefulness under the codebook definition that includes output quality; this is a joint quality preference, not a separately measured feasibility or novelty score.

contrasts.reported: Appendix B.1 says LLM judges favored RAG in eight cases and disagreed in two. Table 6 shows all judges preferring RAG for ideas 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, and 10; all preferring non-RAG for idea 8; and a split for idea 3 (Claude 3.7 and Gemini 2.0 prefer non-RAG; DeepSeek-V3 prefers RAG). No inferential test or uncertainty is reported. The direction denotes more observed preferences for RAG overall, not a statistically established difference or a preference in every case.
contrasts.locator: p. 27, Appendix B.1; p. 28, Table 6; p. 11, Section 4.1 (joint evaluation criteria)

eligibility.reason: S1 meets all three criteria. Individual researchers were randomly assigned to Low, Medium, or Intensive generative-AI configurations for their own research-proposal task (p. 11, Section 5.1; p. 8, Table 3; p. 29, Appendix C.2). The quantitative results analyzed 51 people, 17 per arm, after excluding three extreme survey responses; this is just above the 50-person threshold (p. 13, Section 5.3.1). Actual assignment-stage counts remain null because the source separately identifies only recruited/target and analyzed counts (pp. 12-13, Sections 5.2-5.3.1). Section 6.1 explicitly describes the unique proposals participants created, and Table 4 reports their logged count with hourly means and SDs (pp. 13-14). This qualifies as output fluency under codebook Section 6. The precise rule distinguishing unique proposals from revisions is missing, but the reported measure is explicitly an output count; that reporting gap does not overturn criterion 3. CSI, NASA-TLX, and ownership are self-reports and do not establish output eligibility (p. 12, Section 5.3.1). No across-person output-diversity measure or unassisted post-AI creative task is reported. S2-S3 are model-output benchmarks involving two or three topic providers/evaluators (pp. 27-28, Appendix B), and S4 reports no scored creative-output result (p. 11, Section 4.2). Their participants are not added to S1.

one_line_finding: Among 51 analyzed researchers, unique proposals per hour did not differ significantly across Intensive, Medium, and Low control: means 1.58, 1.88, and 2.19, respectively; F(2, 48) = 1.52, p = 0.22 (p. 14, Table 4; analyzed counts on p. 13, Section 5.3.1).
open_questions: The exact rule for counting unique proposals and distinguishing them from revisions is not stated; Table 4 describes all metrics as function uses per hour, while Section 6.1 interprets this row as generated proposals. Retain the printed hourly normalization without inferring a raw proposal total (pp. 12-14).

Generate_seed_ideas may count function invocations rather than returned ideas. The methods and table caption describe logged actions, and Appendix D shows multiple ideas returned at once. It is retained only in notes, not added as a second output-fluency outcome (pp. 12-14; p. 30, Appendix D).

Actual counts at random assignment are not separately reported: 54 is recruited/target and 18 per condition is the target allocation; 51 total and 17 per condition are the analyzed counts (pp. 12-13, Sections 5.2-5.3.1).

The main procedure and limitations describe 35-40 minutes for proposal generation, whereas the scripted instructions say 30 minutes; the source does not settle which duration was implemented for each participant (pp. 11-12, Section 5.1; p. 21, Section 8.5; p. 29, Appendix C.2).

S2 and S3 do not describe random allocation of people or randomized generation, tool, or presentation order. Their randomized fields remain not_stated, and these two disputed fields remain unresolved (p. 27, Appendix B.1-B.2).

S3 reports three research ideas and individual system ranks but no explicit total of ranked draft observations. Its output-level n_units remains null and this disputed count remains unresolved (pp. 27-28, Appendix B.2 and Table 7).

The protocol-development pilot's analyzed count, condition-order randomization, exact model version, and participant overlap with the other pilots/formal study are not specified. Do not substitute the four design collaborators for an analyzed cohort or add pilot counts to the main sample (p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 11, Section 4.2; p. 27, Appendix B).
The exact number of interviews analyzed after exclusions is not separately stated; the main n_analyzed refers to quantitative analyses (p. 13, Sections 5.3.1-5.3.2).
notes:
Reconciled on 2026-10-09. Both raw forms parsed. Read the complete markdown conversion, including references and Appendices A-F, in chunks, then checked the PDF passages and tables supporting the final facts and retained statistics. PDF page numbers match printed numbering. The saved document is arXiv v1; no later version is assumed. No web requests, effect-size calculations, inferred draft totals, or other file writes were used.

Compared the main design, assignment, arms, participant counts, AI tool/role, task, outcome inventory and coding, statistics/locators, supplement, sample overlap, company involvement, each eligibility criterion, and the one-line result. Equivalent wording and arm-name variants were not counted as disagreements. Four study entries preserve the formal experiment, the two model-output benchmarks, and the protocol-development pilot. S2-S3 human counts denote topic providers/evaluators, not independently assigned intervention participants. S4 has no recoverable analyzed count or scored output outcome.

S1 has one eligible output measure: unique-proposal fluency. Table 4 also lists Generate_seed_ideas, Prompt_full_proposal, Revise_full_proposal, Select_improvements, Query_searches, Select_papers, Prompt_proposal_section, In-line_text_prompting, Save_edits, Provide_feedback, Request_more_critiques, and Customize_improvements. Apart from the ambiguous seed-generation row, these count workflow actions. Generate_seed_ideas hourly means (SDs) are Intensive 6.76 (6.47), Medium 5.02 (3.65), Low 6.31 (4.31), with F(2, 48) = 0.53, p = 0.59 (p. 14, Table 4). Retained from B's notes without assuming invocations equal individual returned ideas. Appendix D says the AI returned four seed ideas in one step (p. 30).

CSI, NASA-TLX, contribution percentages, ownership classifications, and their component/correlation analyses are self-reports, not output creativity scores. For reference only, weighted CSI means (SDs) are Low 59.65 (18.47), Medium 53.13 (17.39), Intensive 63.20 (21.77); Kruskal-Wallis chi-square = 2.08, df = 2, p = 0.353. Unweighted CSI means (SDs), retained from B's notes, are Low 66.79 (11.90), Medium 63.64 (11.87), Intensive 71.51 (15.17); chi-square = 3.735, df = 2, p = 0.155 (p. 14, Table 5). Post-task survey timing does not make these after_ai outcomes.

The pilot judgments assess proposal quality jointly using novelty, feasibility, and impact, so they are coded usefulness (the codebook includes output quality). Separate criterion scores are not supplied. S2-S3 are model_only with AI role other because comparisons score model-generated drafts, not downstream human work after supplied examples. Their contrasts use other; ai_design applies to the randomized human configuration comparison in S1. S2 direction codes summarize the greater number of RAG preferences, without significance or unanimity claims. Table 6 shows a split among judges for idea 3 and unanimous non-RAG preference for idea 8, clarifying the prose that judges disagreed in two cases (pp. 27-28).

S3 gives each draft a rank, so its scored unit is output. Its three ideas are matched topics, not a total of output observations. No total draft count is calculated. Ranks are dependent within idea/researcher. Lower ranks indicate better quality; no effect is computed. Pilot outcomes retain question=none.

Appendix F/Tables 9-10 add Tukey HSD mean differences, p-values, and interval bounds only for Prompt_full_proposal and Select_improvements, not proposal fluency (pp. 30, 32). Appendix D illustrates one member of S1, not an independent sample. No study-data or study-code URL is supplied; software-library links are not study repositories. Appendix D says IRB restrictions prevent publicly sharing full document snapshots and detailed participant edits (p. 29); this does not establish that all other data are unavailable. No outcome was omitted because of the outcome-count cap.

The reconciliation n_unresolved counts disputed fields only. Shared reporting gaps, including the unique-proposal rule, task duration, main assignment-stage counts, and sample overlap, remain explicit in open_questions and are not additional A/B differences.

The assignment, people, and outcome challenge files each contain an empty problems list, so challenge_resolution is empty and all three challenge-action counts are zero; these counts do not count the separate reporting gaps in final.open_items. The unique-proposal count is an eligible fluency outcome; no rated novelty/quality result for S1 is inferred from self-reports or model benchmarks. Every open question and all three unresolved reconciliation differences are addressed in final.open_items. Eligibility-impact flags concern the paper's core inclusion through S1; incomplete S4 assignment/sample details still prevent a full classification of that pilot, which has no reported scored-output result. None of these gaps changes the three confirmed S1 criteria. No separate supplementary-file, posted-data, or study-code URL is supplied to resolve them, so author clarification is identified as the follow-up source without implying that contact occurred. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged. No network requests or effect-size calculations were made.

open_items.item: S1 unique-proposal counting rule (open_questions[0]): the precise distinction between a new proposal and a revision remains unspecified. Section 6.1 explicitly describes proposals participants created, and Table 4 labels the unique-proposal count, so criterion 3 is met despite this reproducibility gap. Author clarification of the logging/deduplication rule would settle it; retain the printed hourly normalization (pp. 12-14, Sections 5.3.1 and 6.1; Table 4).

S1 Generate_seed_ideas counting unit (open_questions[1]): whether this row counts invocations or individual returned ideas remains unresolved. Table 4 describes function uses, and Appendix D illustrates multiple ideas returned together. The row remains in notes, with S1 already qualifying through unique-proposal fluency. Authors would need to define the logged event and its relationship to individual ideas (pp. 12-14, Section 5.3.1 and Table 4; p. 30, Appendix D).

S1 actual counts at random assignment (open_questions[2]): total and arm-specific assignment counts remain unreported. Random assignment is explicit, and criterion 2 uses the confirmed analyzed sample rather than target or recruitment counts. An author-supplied participant flow or allocation record would settle the missing counts (p. 11, Section 5.1; pp. 12-13, Sections 5.2-5.3.1).

S1 implemented task duration (open_questions[3]): the main procedure and limitations state 35-40 minutes, whereas Appendix C.2 says 30 minutes. Appendix D reports approximately 40 minutes for P10 but does not establish timing for every participant. None of the three eligibility criteria requires a particular duration. Author clarification of the implemented protocol and participant timing would settle the discrepancy (pp. 11-12, Section 5.1; p. 21, Section 8.5; p. 29, Appendices C.2 and D).

S2 randomization (part of open_questions[4]; reconciliation.differences: studies[S2].assignment.randomized): the allocation/generation/presentation procedure remains unspecified, so not_stated is retained. This paired model-output benchmark has two topic providers/evaluators and does not supply the qualifying human experiment; randomizing presentation order alone would not establish assignment to human AI assistance. Authors would need to provide the evaluation protocol (p. 27, Appendix B.1).

S3 randomization (part of open_questions[4]; reconciliation.differences: studies[S3].assignment.randomized): allocation and generation/tool/presentation order remain unspecified, so not_stated is retained. This benchmark ranks initial model drafts with three topic providers/evaluators and cannot supply the at-least-50-person experiment. Authors would need to provide the evaluation protocol; S1 eligibility is independently established (pp. 27-28, Appendix B.2 and Table 7).

S3 total ranked-draft observations (open_questions[5]; reconciliation.differences: studies[S3].outcomes[S3-O1].n_units): the paper identifies three research ideas and per-system ranks but does not explicitly print a total of ranked output observations. Retain n_units=null with unit=output. Output counts do not determine the people criterion. Authors would need to confirm the number of drafts included in the rankings (pp. 27-28, Appendix B.2 and Table 7).

S4 pilot reporting and sample overlap (open_questions[6]): analyzed sample size, condition-order randomization, exact model version, and overlap among development pilots and S1 remain unspecified. These limit classification of S4 itself, but S4 reports no scored creative-output result and contributes no participants or estimates to the qualifying S1 study. Authors would need to supply the pilot protocol, participant flow/overlap, and model configuration. The four design collaborators are not substituted for an analyzed cohort (p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 11, Section 4.2; p. 27, Appendix B).

S1 exact number of interviews analyzed (open_questions[7]): the thematic-coding account uses approximate subset counts and does not give a definitive total. Criterion 2 is established by the quantitative analyzed sample, and interview themes are not scored-output outcomes. Authors would need to confirm the interview corpus and any interview exclusions (p. 13, Sections 5.3.1-5.3.2).
